items.answer: Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

questions.question: What two perspectives are used to describe optimization in virtual reality?
options: Visual perception optimization and auditory perception optimization
Augmented reality optimization and mixed reality optimization
Hardware optimization and software optimization
Psychophysiological experience optimization and technological resource utilization
questions.explanation: Optimization in virtual reality can be viewed as optimizing psychophysiological experience or optimizing technological resource utilization.

questions.question: In virtual reality, what does experience optimization roughly mean?
options: Designing the experience to maximize user-controlled navigation
Designing the experience to minimize cybersickness or its possible induction
Designing the experience to reduce resource requirements
Designing the experience to reduce hardware display latency
questions.explanation: Experience optimization in virtual reality is roughly about minimizing cybersickness or the chance that it is induced.

questions.question: Why do high resource requirements matter for virtual reality products?
options: They make immersive experiences more appealing to a wider range of people
They make systems more affordable for the masses
They make mass-market products easier to create
They make systems less affordable and harder to create for mass markets
questions.explanation: Virtual reality and extended reality systems are generally resource-hungry, and too high resource requirements can prevent affordability and mass-market products.

questions.question: What does effective resource optimization in virtual reality require?
options: Maximizing immersive experience regardless of resource requirements
Eliminating all resource requirements without affecting the experience
Balancing trade-offs to reduce resource requirements while preserving immersive experience and quality
Reducing resource requirements by accepting a lower immersive experience
questions.explanation: Effective resource optimization minimizes resource requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it, and ideally without reducing quality.

data.text: VR optimization can be considered from two perspectives: psychophysiological experience and technological resource utilization. Experience optimization can roughly be taken to mean designing the VR experience to minimize cybersickness, while XR systems are generally resource-hungry and may become unaffordable for the masses if requirements are too high. Effective resource optimization requires balancing the trade-offs between minimizing resource requirements and maximizing immersive experience without compromising its quality.
points: VR optimization can be considered from two perspectives: psychophysiological experience and technological resource utilization.
Experience optimization can roughly be taken to mean designing the VR experience to minimize cybersickness.
XR systems are generally resource-hungry, and high resource requirements can make them unaffordable for the masses.
Effective resource optimization involves balancing the trade-off between minimizing resource requirements and maximizing immersive experience without compromising quality.

questions.question: What is cybersickness in virtual reality?
options: A hardware malfunction caused by display resolution
A visually induced motion sickness with multiple contributing factors
A temporary visual defect caused only by field of view
A single-factor effect caused only by visual motion
questions.explanation: Cybersickness, or visually induced motion sickness, can occur during VR use and is not a single-factor effect because many factors can influence it.

questions.question: Which option correctly identifies one internal and one external factor that can induce cybersickness?
options: Latency is internal, and visual motion is external.
User susceptibility to motion sickness is internal, and latency jitter is external.
Field of view is internal, and emotional condition is external.
Display resolution is internal, and the user's age is external.
questions.explanation: User susceptibility to motion sickness is listed among internal factors, while latency jitter is listed among hardware factors in external factors.

questions.question: Why can cybersickness mitigation strategies sometimes reduce presence?
options: They may reduce the difference between the virtual and physical environments.
They may make the environment feel more artificial and less immersive.
They may make the user feel less aware of the artificial environment.
They may make the environment feel more real and more immersive.
questions.explanation: Reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real one and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

questions.question: What is the central challenge when developing cybersickness mitigation strategies?
options: Maximizing all hardware specifications.
Eliminating every source of visual motion.
Reducing only the user's exposure duration.
Avoiding any compromise to presence.
questions.explanation: The challenge is to develop mitigation strategies while avoiding compromising presence, which is indirectly related to user experience.

data.text: Cybersickness is a multi-factor condition caused by various internal user factors and external hardware or content factors. While reducing this sickness is important for improving the user experience, mitigation strategies can often compromise the sense of presence by making the environment feel artificial. The primary challenge is to develop solutions that mitigate cybersickness without compromising the user's sense of presence.
points: Cybersickness is a multi-factor condition that can affect individuals interacting with VR.
The condition is caused by internal factors like user susceptibility and external factors like hardware and VR content.
Reducing cybersickness is important to improve the user experience and make VR more appealing.
Mitigation strategies can often come at the cost of presence by making the environment feel more artificial.
The challenge is to develop mitigation strategies that do not compromise the sense of presence.

questions.question: In VR experience optimization, reducing which factors can minimize cybersickness while preserving presence?
options: Cognitive demand or visual complexity
Exposure duration or navigation distance
Optic-flow speed or field of view
Display latency or display resolution
questions.explanation: Cybersickness is minimized by reducing either the duration of exposure to the virtual world or the distance covered during navigation, while presence is preserved or maximized.

questions.question: Which VR locomotion technique category includes full gait, partial gait, and gait negation methods involving physical walking?
options: Selection-based techniques
Manipulation-based techniques
Steering-based techniques
Walking-based techniques
questions.explanation: Virtual locomotion techniques involving physical walking are walking-based techniques, which include full gait, partial gait, and gait negation.

questions.question: What is the key difference between system-controlled and user-controlled VR tours?
options: The system controls the user's movement
The user selects the next movement target
The user controls the navigation path
The user steers the virtual avatar
questions.explanation: In a user-controlled tour, the user controls how and where to navigate, while in a system-controlled tour the system controls the user's movement.

questions.question: Why can a system-controlled VR tour have reduced cognitive demands?
options: The user must plan each navigation step
The user continuously chooses a movement target
The system decides how and where the user moves
The user must adjust the locomotion speed
questions.explanation: System-controlled tours reduce cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves, allowing the user to focus on the experience.

questions.question: Why can lack of user involvement in a system-controlled VR tour undermine presence?
options: The user has too many movement choices
The user can choose a new path at will
The user is unable to control the movement
The user controls movement with controllers
questions.explanation: Lack of user involvement makes system-controlled tours less realistic and defeats presence because the user cannot control the movement.

data.text: Cybersickness is minimized by reducing navigation duration or distance while preserving presence. Virtual locomotion techniques are categorized into walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based techniques. VR tours are categorized into user-controlled and system-controlled tours. System-controlled tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands, but they are less realistic and can defeat the purpose of presence.
points: Cybersickness is minimized by reducing navigation duration or distance while preserving presence.
Virtual locomotion techniques are categorized into walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based techniques.
VR tours are categorized into user-controlled and system-controlled tours.
System-controlled tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands, but they are less realistic and can defeat the purpose of presence.

questions.question: In a VR tour, what does a system-controlled tour mean?
options: The system forces the user to move from one place to another.
The user controls the movement with a hand controller.
The user chooses each destination before the tour.
The user stays in place while the system changes the scene.
questions.explanation: A system-controlled tour is a navigation mode in which the system, not the user, moves the user from one place to another.

questions.question: Why is a realistic walking experience important in a system-controlled VR tour?
options: It requires the user to walk at a constant speed.
It lets the user ignore the realism of the walking motion.
It makes the user feel more aware of system control.
It helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system.
questions.explanation: Realistic walking helps the user feel present instead of being controlled and reduces awareness of unrealistic elements.

questions.question: What is optic flow in a VR tour?
options: The user's real-world walking speed.
The number of visual objects in the scene.
The speed at which the visual scene changes.
The distance between two places in the VR tour.
questions.explanation: Optic flow is the speed of change in the visual scene through which movement is perceived.

questions.question: When a system-controlled VR tour assumes walking, what should its optic flow match?
options: The user's instantaneous real-world walking speed.
The speed of the system-controlled tour path.
The user's preferred VR walking speed.
A single constant scene-change speed.
questions.explanation: The scene-change speed should match the user's real-world walking speed, and a model of typical walking behavior can make it follow the user's instantaneous walking speed.

questions.question: Why is a constant optic flow not very realistic in a system-controlled walking tour?
options: Because users cannot perceive scene-change speed.
Because the virtual scene does not change continuously.
Because people rarely walk at constant speed.
Because system-controlled tours require a fixed movement speed.
questions.explanation: A more realistic tour uses a walking-behavior model because people rarely walk at a constant speed, so constant optic flow is less realistic.

data.text: System-controlled tours are navigation modes where the system forces the user to move. Although realistic walking helps users feel present, it is difficult to achieve in automated tours that lack continuous user input. To make movement look realistic, the optic flow should match real-world walking speeds rather than VR walking speeds. Because people rarely walk at constant speeds, the optic flow must be matched to the user's instantaneous walking speed.
points: System-controlled tours are navigation modes where the system forces the user to move.
Realistic walking is important for feeling present, but it is difficult to achieve in automated tours that lack continuous user input.
Optic flow should match real-world walking speeds rather than VR walking speeds to appear realistic.
Optic flow must match the user's instantaneous walking speed because people rarely walk at constant speeds.

questions.question: Why can a virtual reality optimization choice that lowers cybersickness still weaken the immersive experience, and why does that matter for user experience?
questions.reference_answer: In virtual reality, experience optimization is often about designing the experience to minimize cybersickness. Cybersickness mitigation strategies can make the environment feel more artificial, so they may reduce presence, which is the psychological side of perceiving immersive qualities. Because presence is indirectly related to user experience, the challenge is to reduce sickness without compromising presence.

questions.question: Why can a system-controlled virtual reality tour feel easier for a user while also making presence harder to achieve, and how can a realistic walking experience address that problem?
questions.reference_answer: A system-controlled virtual reality tour is a tour where the system controls the user's movement, often along a predetermined path. It can feel effortless and reduce cognitive demands because the user does not decide how or where to move, but this lack of user involvement makes it less realistic and can defeat presence. A realistic walking experience helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system and reduces awareness of unrealistic elements.

questions.question: Why should a system-controlled virtual reality tour that simulates walking match the user's real-world walking speed rather than a constant virtual walking speed, and why is instantaneous matching more realistic?
questions.reference_answer: System-controlled tours typically do not allow continuous user input, so it is difficult to align user input with walking speed or to judge whether the speed provided by the system is natural. Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and user movement in a virtual reality tour appears as a constantly changing scene. If the tour assumes walking, its optic flow should match the user's actual or typical real-world walking speed rather than virtual reality walking speed; constant optic flow is not very realistic because people rarely walk at constant speed, so a more realistic tour matches instantaneous walking speed using a walking speed model.

questions.question: Why does technological optimization in virtual reality connect resource requirements with affordable mass-market products, and how must it be balanced with immersive experience?
questions.reference_answer: Virtual reality optimization can be considered from the perspective of technological optimization, which in virtual reality concerns resource requirements and immersive experience. Extended reality and virtual reality systems are generally resource-hungry, and if their resource requirements are too high, products will not be affordable for the masses. Effective resource optimization therefore means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience without compromising it, which requires balancing the trade-off between resource requirements and immersive experience.
